title: Russia's UAV Campaign Over Europe
date_evidence: Russia's UAV Campaign over Europe; Authors: Charlie Edwards, Rex Fox O'Loughlin and Louis Bearn; Publication Date: 2nd July 2026
key_claim: Between August 2024 and February 2026 UAVs flew in the airspace of a dozen NATO member states and Ireland (144 recorded incidents across 13 states), forcing repeated closures of major airports, disrupting military operations and penetrating sensitive defence installations; the campaign exposed gaps in detection, decision-making and legal authority, and the report concludes that 'as long as rules of engagement remain fragmented across national jurisdictions, the Kremlin will continue to exploit them. No amount of hardware will compensate for the absence of political authority to use it.' The proposed European Drone Defence Initiative will not be functional for years and only engages drones once inside European airspace, with no mandate over the shadow-fleet vessels that launch them.
frame_summary: IISS argues that Europe's counter-drone failure is fundamentally a problem of fragmented legal authority and command (plus maritime accountability for shadow-fleet launch platforms), not primarily of hardware, and that buying more counter-UAV kit without unified rules of engagement will not restore deterrence.
notes: Primary anchor for the authority-gap signal. Report by Charlie Edwards, Rex Fox O'Loughlin, Louis Bearn. IISS research-paper URL path shows 2026/06; publication and coverage cluster at 2 July 2026 (AeroTime, unmannedairspace, ABC). Numeric provenance for the 144-incident / 48-18-26 split held in the AeroTime record's verbatim_quote.

title: Russia likely used shadow fleet ships for drone campaign over Europe: IISS
key_claim: Reporting the IISS dataset: 144 incidents across 13 European states, approximately 48% over military facilities, 18% over civilian airports and 26% over critical infrastructure such as ports and energy sites; reported incidents jumped from an average of four per month to 22.5 per month between September and December 2025, with Germany alone recording 58 sightings; despite Operation Eastern Sentry and new shootdown authorisations in Germany, Lithuania and Romania, the report warns governments not to 'mistake activity for achievement', and the EDDI 'drone wall' only engages drones once they enter European airspace.
frame_summary: AeroTime reports the IISS findings, foregrounding that Europe's air-defence architecture was built for conventional threats and that fragmented legal authorities, uneven detection and slow attribution leave the continent exposed even as spending and initiatives multiply.
verbatim_quote: The report, led by IISS senior fellow Charlie Edwards, compiles a dataset of 144 incidents across 13 European states. Approximately 48% of sightings occurred over military facilities, 18% over civilian airports, and 26% over critical infrastructure such as ports and energy sites. Reported incidents jumped from an average of four per month to 22.5 per month between September and December 2025, with Germany alone recording 58 sightings.

title: Who has authority to deal with drones? In most of Europe, that's unclear
key_claim: Drawing on primary research (23 stakeholder interviews across Britain and Europe by Challenger Research with TWA), the piece argues Europe's drone problem is a governance problem: the hardware exists, but legal authority, jurisdictional clarity and political will are missing. Drone-related disruptions at European airports more than tripled between January 2024 and November 2025; the interval between detection and disruption at an airport is less than five minutes, yet few airports hold legal authority to act; across ports, energy networks and data infrastructure, critical national infrastructure operators can detect hostile UAS activity but are legally barred from taking active countermeasures; Poland's effects-based Operation SAN empowers police, border guard and armed forces simultaneously while most states remain fragmented, and stakeholders describe 'rules of engagement' as the primary issue with 'no ownership of responsibility'.
frame_summary: ASPI/Challenger Research argues that the binding constraint on European counter-drone response is not technology but the legal authority and jurisdictional clarity to use it, and that Europe should build a binding common counter-drone legal architecture in advance of a crisis rather than in reaction to one.
verbatim_quote: Drone-related disruptions at European airports more than tripled between January 2024 and November 2025. Our research has found that the interval between detection and disruption at an airport is less than five minutes, yet few airports hold the legal authority to act on what they have detected.
notes: Core frame source for the authority-gap thesis and the critical-infrastructure-operator dimension. ASPI is a think tank; The Strategist hosts the commissioned Challenger Research primary study (23 stakeholder interviews). Classified Tier 2 as institutional research. title: Commission publishes the Action Plan on Drone and Counter-Drone Security
date_evidence: News article - 11 February 2026 - Directorate-General for Defence Industry and Space; Publication date 11 February 2026
key_claim: On 11 February 2026 the Commission published the Action Plan on Drone and Counter-Drone Security, designed to support Member States through coordinated actions that complement (not replace) national measures, focused on preparedness, detection, coordinating responses and defence readiness; it underpins the European Drone Defence Initiative and Eastern Flank Watch flagged in the Defence Readiness Roadmap 2030, and proposes that Member States appoint National Drone Security Coordinators to oversee national implementation.
frame_summary: The Commission frames counter-drone as a coordination, funding and industrial-readiness problem it can convene and support, while active response and the legal authority to engage drones remain national competences, so Brussels organises the response without resolving the engagement-authority question.
notes: Single permitted structural anchor (3-6m band, 154 days). Canonical primary source for the EU-level coordination response that the signal contrasts against national engagement authority.

title: Drohnenabwehr: Was darf die Bundeswehr?
key_claim: German defence-law expert Dr Christian Richter (GIDS) explains the amended Luftsicherheitsgesetz (LuftSiG s.15a II; in force after Bundesrat approval in early March 2026, BGBl I 2026, 68): the armed forces may now explicitly use weapons or other means against unmanned aircraft to prevent an especially serious incident; the Laender police and Bundespolizei remain primary, with the Bundeswehr handling large drones the police cannot via Amtshilfe (Art. 35 II 2 GG); a new Drohnenabwehrkompetenzzentrum pools BKA, Bundespolizei, Land police and Bundeswehr; drones may be shot down only where there is an immediate danger to human life or critical infrastructure, and airborne shootdown remains an ultima ratio over a densely populated country.
frame_summary: A German defence-law expert argues the LuftSiG reform closes a specific legal gap by extending military engagement authority into domestic airspace as a tightly bounded ultima ratio, resolved through shared civil-military coordination rather than a wholesale militarisation of policing.
verbatim_quote: Drohnen dürfen abgeschossen werden, wenn unmittelbare Gefahr für Menschenleben oder kritische Infrastruktur droht.
notes: German-language source (multi-language discipline for a European topic). Primary-jurisdiction legal detail on the German engagement-authority reform.
